newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Rains sweep Czech Republic, raising flood fears.
newsitem.headline: Rains sweep Czech Republic, raising flood fears.

text.p: Rain swept across the Czech Republic on Friday, raising fears that storms forecast for the weekend could trigger a new wave of the flooding that has killed more than 40 people.
Forecasters said river levels in the flood-battered east were receding but that, with the ground saturated and rain already falling, they were likely to rise rapidly.
"If the rainfall is intense, which is very realistic, there might be more flooding but I am not able to estimate the extent," Michal Veverka of the Czech Hydrological Centre told Reuters.

The prospect of more rain also put neighbouring Poland, where floods have killed 48 people in the past two weeks, on renewed alert as several rivers running through the south of the country rise in the Czech Republic.
Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz telephoned Czech Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec on Thursday to discuss efforts to combat the floods, a Czech diplomatic source said.
A Polish government spokeswoman said last week the Czechs had emptied reservoirs on the Odra river, which runs though Poland, and that this had worsened the situation there.
But Polish Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati, visiting Prague, said no official criticism was implied.
He said the two countries had been coordinating flood efforts since last week, including releasing water on the Odra.

"We have been in constant working contact with the Czech authorities. In this respect, we have been permanently informed of the situation there and the Czech authorities tell us when they want to release some water," Rosati told a news conference with Zieleniec and Hungarian Foreign Minister Laszlo Kovacs.
"I think the cooperation is going very well," he said.
Czech flood prevention teams were working to repair breached defences in anticipation of a fresh onslaught, Czech Television reported.

Rain began falling overnight but storms were forecast for the flood-hit areas over the weekend, the Czech Weather Service said. Up to 100 millimetres (four inches) could fall in the mountains in the next 24 hours, and an average 30 millimetres in low-lying areas, the service said.
Police put the latest death toll in the worst flooding to hit the region in a century at 45, one fewer than Thursday, but two people are still missing.

Thousands of houses have been destroyed or badly damaged, road, rail and telecommunications links have been cut and valuable industrial and agricultural land has been swamped, making the floods a major financial disaster for the country of 10.5 million people.
Economists are still tallying the cost of the floods but some have put overall damage at up to 100 billion crowns.
The government has offered compensation for flood victims and has drawn up plans for bond issues and other steps to finance the relief effort.
It is also considering a soft loan of more than 10 billion crowns, which has been offered by the European Union's European Investment Bank.
